claim: Different phospholipid species are segregated between the inner and outer leaflets of the plasma membrane by ATP-dependent lipid transporters from bacteria to mammals.
source: From bacteria to mammals, different phospholipid species are segregated between the inner and outer leaflets of the plasma membrane by ATP-dependent lipid transporters.
evidence: This is a statement presented in the abstract as established background knowledge about membrane biology.

claim: The surface hydrophilic transmembrane cavity exposed to the lipid bilayer on the fungal scramblase nhTMEM16 serves as the pathway for both lipid translocation and ion conduction across the membrane.
source: Using MD simulations coupled with experimental assays, we show that the surface hydrophilic transmembrane cavity exposed to the lipid bilayer on the fungal scramblase nhTMEM16 serves as the pathway for both lipid translocation and ion conduction across the membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by both MD simulation data and experimental assays described in the manuscript.

claim: Ca2+ binding stimulates the open conformation of nhTMEM16 by altering the structure of transmembrane helices that line the cavity.
source: Ca2+ binding stimulates its open conformation by altering the structure of transmembrane helices that line the cavity.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data comparing Ca2+-activated and Ca2+-free states.

claim: Mutation of two residues in the pore region of the TMEM16A Ca2+-activated Cl- channel converts it into a robust scramblase.
source: We have identified key amino acids necessary for phospholipid scrambling and validated the idea that ions permeate TMEM16 Cl- channels via a structurally homologous pathway by showing that mutation of two residues in the pore region of the TMEM16A Ca2+-activated Cl- channel convert it into a robust scramblase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that specific mutations in TMEM16A confer scramblase activity.

claim: Dissipation of phospholipid asymmetry in response to elevated cytoplasmic Ca2+ concentration is a ubiquitous signaling mechanism critical for diverse cellular events including blood coagulation, bone mineralization, and cell-cell interaction.
source: Dissipation of this asymmetry in response to the elevation of cytoplasmic Ca2+ concentration is a ubiquitous signaling mechanism critical for diverse cellular events including blood coagulation, bone mineralization, and cell-cell interaction (Fadok et al., 1992; Fadok et al., 2001; Sahu et al., 2007; Bratton and Henson, 2008; Sanyal and Menon, 2009; Bevers and Williamson, 2016; Nagata et al., 2016; Pomorski and Menon, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Phospholipid scrambling is mediated by phospholipid scramblases, which harvest the energy of the phospholipid gradient to drive the nonspecific and bidirectional transport of phospholipids between leaflets.
source: Phospholipid scrambling is mediated by phospholipid scramblases, which harvest the energy of the phospholipid gradient to drive the nonspecific and bidirectional transport of phospholipids between leaflets.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the mechanism of phospholipid scramblases.

claim: Proteins responsible for Ca2+-activated lipid scrambling belong to the anoctamin/TMEM16 superfamily.
source: Proteins responsible for Ca2+-activated lipid scrambling belong to the anoctamin/TMEM16 superfamily (Suzuki et al., 2010, 2013; Pedemonte and Galietta, 2014; Picollo et al., 2015; Brunner et al., 2016; Whitlock and Hartzell, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Among the ten mammalian TMEM16 paralogs, TMEM16C, D, F, G, and J have been identified as Ca2+-activated phospholipid scramblases.
source: Among the ten mammalian TMEM16 paralogs, TMEM16C, D, F, G, and J have been identified as Ca2+-activated phospholipid scramblases while TMEM16A and TMEM16B are Ca2+-activated Cl− channels (CaCCs).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the TMEM16 family.

claim: TMEM16A and TMEM16B are Ca2+-activated Cl− channels.
source: Among the ten mammalian TMEM16 paralogs, TMEM16C, D, F, G, and J have been identified as Ca2+-activated phospholipid scramblases while TMEM16A and TMEM16B are Ca2+-activated Cl− channels (CaCCs).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the TMEM16 family.

claim: The fungal nhTMEM16 is a homodimer with 10 transmembrane helices in each subunit.
source: nhTMEM16 is a homodimer with 10 transmembrane helices in each subunit.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure of nhTMEM16.

claim: The nhTMEM16 protein exhibits an unusual ~10 Å wide hydrophilic cavity on the surface of each subunit.
source: The protein exhibits an unusual ~10 Å wide hydrophilic cavity on the surface of each subunit.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The subunit cavity in nhTMEM16 is formed by transmembrane helices TM3-TM7.
source: This subunit cavity is formed by transmembrane (TM) helices TM3-TM7.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The helices that border the cavity (TM4 and TM6) in nhTMEM16 are amphipathic, with polar and charged residues facing the cavity.
source: The helices that border the cavity (TM4 and TM6) are amphipathic, with polar and charged residues facing the cavity.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: Brunner et al. (2014) proposed that the hydrophilic cavity provides a pathway for phospholipid head groups to move between membrane leaflets during scrambling while the fatty acid tails remain in the hydrophobic bilayer.
source: Brunner et al. (2014) proposed that the hydrophilic cavity provides a pathway for phospholipid head groups to move between membrane leaflets during scrambling while the fatty acid tails remain in the hydrophobic bilayer.
evidence: This claim is attributed to a prior publication by Brunner et al.

claim: The mechanism of phospholipid scrambling through the hydrophilic cavity is predicted by molecular dynamics simulations.
source: This mechanism is also predicted by molecular dynamics simulations (Stansfeld et al., 2015; Bethel and Grabe, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior MD simulation studies.

claim: A highly conserved Ca2+-binding site for two Ca2+ ions is located near the cytoplasmic end of the aqueduct in nhTMEM16.
source: A highly conserved Ca2+-binding site for two Ca2+ ions is located near the cytoplasmic end of the aqueduct.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: Equivalent residues in the Ca2+-binding site are responsible for Ca2+ activation of both TMEM16 phospholipid scramblases and ion channels.
source: Equivalent residues are responsible for Ca2+ activation of both TMEM16 phospholipid scramblases and ion channels (Yu et al., 2012; Malvezzi et al., 2013; Brunner et al., 2014; Tien et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: nhTMEM16 causes a distortion in the distribution of bilayer phospholipids due to hydrophobic mismatch between the protein and the membrane.
source: This staggering of the transmembrane protein hydrophobicity causes a distortion in the distribution of bilayer phospholipids due to their tendency to match the hydrophobic surface of the protein (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by MD simulation data and visualization in Figure 1A.

claim: The distortion caused by nhTMEM16 reduces the membrane thickness near the aqueduct and produces a bend in the bilayer centered on the aqueduct.
source: This not only reduces the membrane thickness near the aqueduct but also produces a bend in the bilayer centered on the aqueduct so that the membrane is high on the TM4 side and low on the TM6 side of the aqueduct.
evidence: This is based on analysis of MD simulation data.

claim: Membrane thinning caused by nhTMEM16 primes lipid translocation by reducing the energy required to move a lipid across the membrane.
source: Because the rate of diffusion of a molecule across the membrane is inversely related to the distance (Fick's Law), membrane thinning will prime lipid translocation by reducing the energy required to move a lipid across the membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on Fick's Law and the observed membrane thinning.

claim: Membrane bending may favor non-bilayer phases that facilitate scrambling.
source: Membrane bending may also favor non-bilayer phases that facilitate scrambling.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential effect of membrane bending.

claim: Spontaneous penetration of lipid head groups into the membrane interior along the aqueduct was observed in MD simulations, resulting in a continuous file of lipids connecting the outer and inner leaflets.
source: Spontaneous penetration of lipid head groups into the membrane interior along the aqueduct was observed, resulting in a continuous file of lipids connecting the outer and inner leaflets (Figure 2A middle and right panels; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by MD simulation data and visualization in Figure 2A.

claim: Each aqueduct in nhTMEM16 contained an average of 3.3 phospholipid phosphates in its central 20 Å-thick core during the simulation.
source: Each aqueduct contained an average of 3.3 phospholipid phosphates in its central 20 Å-thick core and accommodated up to six phosphates (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data shown in Figure 2.

claim: During the last 500 ns of the simulation, the aqueduct was occupied by >4 phosphates ~40% of the time.
source: During the last 500 ns of the simulation, the aqueduct was occupied by >4 phosphates ~40% of the time (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The structure of nhTMEM16 converged on a stable conformation after 150 ns of the simulation with a heavy-atom RMSD of 3.6 ± 0.4 Å for the transmembrane domains compared to the crystal structure.
source: The structure had converged on a stable conformation after 150 ns of the simulation and exhibited a heavy-atom RMSD of 3.6 ± 0.4 Å for the transmembrane domains compared to the crystal structure.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data.

claim: While phospholipid head groups were wedged in the aqueduct, their flexible hydrocarbon tails remained in the hydrophobic phase of the membrane.
source: While phospholipid head groups were wedged in the aqueduct, their flexible hydrocarbon tails remained in the hydrophobic phase of the membrane (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of MD simulation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: One complete translocation of a lipid from the inner leaflet to the outer leaflet was observed during the simulation.
source: This event represented a full permeation of the lipid from the inner leaflet to the outer leaflet (Figure 3—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on observation in MD simulation data shown in videos.

claim: Four more full translocations were observed when voltage was applied in the simulations.
source: While we observed only one full translocation under conditions of zero voltage across the bilayer, we have observed four more full translocations when voltage was applied as described later.
evidence: This is based on observation in MD simulation data with applied voltage.

claim: The lipid tails underwent ~170 degrees of rotation as the head group shifted from one leaflet to the other along the aqueduct during the complete translocation.
source: In the one complete translocation that we observed, the lipid tails underwent ~170 degrees of rotation as the head group shifted from one leaflet to the other along the aqueduct (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Three most visited sites for lipid phosphate groups within the aqueduct are named 'internal site (Sint)', 'central site (Scen)', and 'external site (Sext)'.
source: The three most visited sites are named 'internal site (Sint)', 'central site (Scen)', and 'external site (Sext)'.
evidence: This is based on analysis of phosphate occupancy density from MD simulation data.

claim: The T333V mutation in nhTMEM16 greatly reduced phospholipid scrambling.
source: In contrast to the robust scrambling observed with WT nhTMEM16 in the presence of Ca2+, very little scrambling was observed in cells expressing T333V or N378K mutants of nhTMEM16 (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: The N378K mutation in nhTMEM16 greatly reduced phospholipid scrambling.
source: In contrast to the robust scrambling observed with WT nhTMEM16 in the presence of Ca2+, very little scrambling was observed in cells expressing T333V or N378K mutants of nhTMEM16 (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: The R505Q mutation in nhTMEM16 greatly reduced phospholipid scrambling.
source: The R505Q mutation greatly reduced phospholipid scrambling (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: The fungal TMEM16 scramblases nhTMEM16 and afTMEM16 as well as the mammalian scramblase TMEM16F conduct ions as well as scramble lipids.
source: It has been reported that the fungal TMEM16 scramblases nhTMEM16 (Brunner et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2016) and afTMEM16 (Malvezzi et al., 2013) as well as the mammalian scramblase TMEM16F (Yu et al., 2015) (and references therein) conduct ions as well as scramble lipids (Whitlock and Hartzell, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: nhTMEM16 elicited phospholipid scrambling and ionic currents when intracellular Ca2+ was elevated.
source: nhTMEM16 elicited phospholipid scrambling and ionic currents when intracellular Ca2+ was elevated (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: WT nhTMEM16 ionic current activated by 200 µM free Ca2+ exhibited a linear current-voltage relationship that reversed at ~0 mV under symmetrical ionic conditions.
source: WT nhTMEM16 ionic current activated by 200 µM free Ca2+ exhibited a linear current-voltage relationship that reversed at ~0 mV under symmetrical ionic conditions.
evidence: This is based on experimental electrophysiology data.

claim: Upon 10-fold reduction in NaCl, the reversal potential of nhTMEM16 shifted −7 mV, which corresponds to PNa:PCl = 2.3 ± 0.2.
source: Upon 10-fold reduction in NaCl, Erev shifted −7 mV (Figure 5B), which corresponds to PNa:PCl = 2.3 ± 0.2 as calculated by the Goldman, Hodgkin, Katz equation (Figure 5 C).
evidence: This is based on experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: The PCs:PCl of nhTMEM16 was 1.5 ± 0.1.
source: PCs:PCl was 1.5 ± 0.1.
evidence: This is based on experimental electrophysiology data.

claim: The currents associated with nhTMEM16 scrambling are slightly cation-selective.
source: Therefore, the currents associated with nhTMEM16 scrambling are slightly cation-selective.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured permeability ratios.

claim: Ionic currents were greatly reduced in cells expressing nhTMEM16 mutants T333V, N378K, and R505Q that exhibit reduced scrambling.
source: Our suggestion that ionic currents are linked to phospholipid scrambling is supported by the observation that ionic currents were greatly reduced in cells expressing nhTMEM16 mutants T333V, N378K, and R505Q that exhibit reduced scrambling (Figure 5 D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The TMEM16F Q559K mutation greatly reduced scrambling and ionic currents.
source: When TMEM16F Q559 (homologous to nhTMEM16 N378) was mutated to the corresponding TMEM16A residue (Q559K), scrambling and ionic currents were greatly reduced (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Replacing TMEM16F Q559 with the corresponding amino acid from nhTMEM16 (Q559N) did not abrogate scrambling by TMEM16F.
source: As expected, replacing TMEM16F Q559 with the corresponding amino acid from nhTMEM16 (Q559N) did not abrogate scrambling by TMEM16F (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mutating S514 in TMEM16F to the corresponding nhTMEM16 amino acid (S514T) had no effect on scrambling.
source: Mutating S514 in TMEM16F to the corresponding nhTMEM16 amino acid (S514T) had no effect on scrambling, as expected.
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: The S514V mutation in TMEM16F had little effect on scrambling.
source: We initially expected that replacing TMEM16F S514 with V from TMEM16A would abrogate scrambling, but the S514V mutation had little effect on scrambling.
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: Cells expressing TMEM16A mutants V543T or V543S exhibited robust phospholipid scrambling.
source: Fewer than 20% of the WT TMEM16A-expressing cells exhibited scramblase activity within 15 min of cytosolic Ca2+ elevation (Figure 6B and D), but cells expressing TMEM16A mutants V543T or V543S exhibited robust phospholipid scrambling in the same time period (Figure 6D), consistent with the hypothesis that this amino acid plays a key role in conducting lipids across the bilayer.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6B and D.

claim: Replacing TMEM16A K588 with the corresponding nhTMEM16 amino acid N (K588N) induced robust phospholipid scrambling.
source: Replacing TMEM16A K588 with the corresponding nhTMEM16 amino acid N (K588N) also induced robust phospholipid scrambling (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Replacing K588 in TMEM16A with the corresponding TMEM16F amino acid Q did not induce scrambling.
source: However, replacing K588 with the corresponding TMEM16F amino acid Q did not induce scrambling.
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: The V543S mutation in TMEM16A changed the ionic selectivity of TMEM16A.
source: In addition to conferring scramblase activity on TMEM16A, the V543S mutation also changed the ionic selectivity of TMEM16A (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is based on experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Immediately after initiating whole-cell recording, TMEM16A V543S currents were strongly Cl- selective with PCl/PCs = 9.7.
source: Immediately after initiating whole-cell recording, TMEM16A V543S currents were strongly Cl- selective, because switching from extracellular 150 mM CsCl to 10 mM CsCl caused a +45 mV shift of Erev corresponding to PCl/PCs = 9.7 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: As phospholipid scrambling developed in TMEM16A V543S, the ionic current became weakly cation-selective with PCl/PCs = 0.45.
source: With time, the reversal potential changed as phospholipid scrambling developed. The ionic current became weakly cation-selective as evidenced by a −17 mV negative shift in Erev upon switching from 150 mM CsCl to 10 mM CsCl. This corresponds to a 21-fold decrease in anion selectivity (PCl/PCs = 0.45) (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: With the imposition of transmembrane potentials, the number of lipid head groups in the central 20 Å-thick core of membrane increased from 3.3 at 0 mV to 3.4 at −150/−250 mV, and 4.0 at −500 mV.
source: With the imposition of transmembrane potentials, the number of lipid head groups in the central 20 Å-thick core of membrane increased from 3.3 at 0 mV to 3.4 at −150/−250 mV, and 4.0 at −500 mV.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data with applied voltage.

claim: Na+ permeation from the extracellular side to the intracellular side of the membrane was observed to occur through the aqueduct in MD simulations with applied voltage.
source: Further, Na+ permeation from the extracellular side to the intracellular side of the membrane was observed to occur through the aqueduct.
evidence: This is based on observation in MD simulation data with applied voltage.

claim: At −150 mV and −250 mV, Na+ permeation events occurred in both subunits during the 700 ns simulations.
source: At −150 mV and −250 mV, Na+ permeation events occurred in both subunits during the 700 ns simulations.
evidence: This is based on observation in MD simulation data with applied voltage.

claim: The average coordination number of permeant Na+ ions during the course of ion translocation was 5.70 ± 0.51.
source: The average coordination number of permeant Na+ ions during the course of ion translocation was 5.70 ± 0.51 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Coordination of permeant Na+ ions is supplied mainly by oxygen atoms from water molecules (83.4%).
source: Coordination is supplied mainly by oxygen atoms from water molecules (83.4%).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data.

claim: The remainder of Na+ coordination was split between protein (62.5%) and lipid (37.5%).
source: The remainder was split between protein (62.5%) and lipid (37.5%) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: T333 is the residue that interacts most extensively (with a time percentage of 36.8%) with permeant Na+ ions.
source: Intriguingly, T333, which is a key gating residue for lipid scrambling, is the residue that interacts most extensively (with a time percentage of 36.8%) with permeant Na+ ions.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data.

claim: At −500 mV there were 24 Na+ influx events over 700 ns in the MD simulation.
source: The probability of Na+ permeation increased with voltage. At −500 mV there were 24 Na+ influx events over 700 ns (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Figure 7—video 1) and at −1000 mV there were 38 Na+ influx and 8 Cl- efflux events over 90 ns of simulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on observation in MD simulation data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: At −1000 mV there were 38 Na+ influx and 8 Cl- efflux events over 90 ns of simulation.
source: The probability of Na+ permeation increased with voltage. At −500 mV there were 24 Na+ influx events over 700 ns (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Figure 7—video 1) and at −1000 mV there were 38 Na+ influx and 8 Cl- efflux events over 90 ns of simulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on observation in MD simulation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The aqueduct dilates during the frequent ion permeation phase in the simulation at −500 mV.
source: Importantly, the aqueduct as measured by the center-of-mass (COM) distance between TM4 and TM6 dilates during the frequent ion permeation phase in the simulation (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on analysis of MD simulation data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: Five full lipid permeation events (2 POPS and 3 POPC) from the inner leaflet to the outer leaflet were observed in a combined simulation trajectory with a total aggregate time of 1700 ns.
source: To analyze lipid scrambling in the presence of a transmembrane voltage, a combined simulation trajectory with a total aggregate time of 1700 ns (1000 ns at 0 mV, followed by 700 ns at −500 mV) was used. Five full lipid permeation events (2 POPS and 3 POPC) from the inner leaflet to the outer leaflet were observed (Figure 8A and B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on observation in MD simulation data shown in Figure 8A, B, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: For the full POPS permeation events, R505 interacted with the head group for 59–80% of the scrambling time.
source: For the full POPS permeation events, the head groups were well coordinated by protein oxygen and nitrogen atoms (Figure 8A). The POPS head group interacts most closely with R505 (59–80% of the scrambling time).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: E496 and N378 also contribute significantly (>10% of the scrambling time) to POPS head group coordination.
source: E496 and N378 also contribute significantly (>10% of the scrambling time).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data.

claim: The scrambled POPS head group is coordinated by at least two oxygen/nitrogen atoms from the protein an average of ~49% of the time during its transit.
source: The scrambled POPS head group is coordinated by at least two oxygen/nitrogen atoms from the protein an average of ~49% of the time during its transit (Figure 8C top panel, Figure 8—figure supplement 2); while for POPC, the average probability is only ~5% (Figure 8C bottom panel).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: For POPC, the average probability of coordination by at least two oxygen/nitrogen atoms from the protein is only ~5%.
source: The scrambled POPS head group is coordinated by at least two oxygen/nitrogen atoms from the protein an average of ~49% of the time during its transit (Figure 8C top panel, Figure 8—figure supplement 2); while for POPC, the average probability is only ~5% (Figure 8C bottom panel).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Three residues inside the aqueduct (E496, R505 and R548) coordinate POPS more strongly than POPC.
source: Three residues inside the aqueduct (E496, R505 and R548) coordinate (coordination ratio >0.2) POPS more strongly than POPC (Figure 8D, Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of MD simulation data shown in Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: Lipid occupancy of the aqueduct did not occur when Ca2+ was removed in the simulation.
source: In contrast to the Ca2+-activated simulation, lipid occupancy of the aqueduct did not occur when Ca2+ was removed.
evidence: This is based on comparison of MD simulation data with and without Ca2+.

claim: On average only 1.8 lipids were present in the aqueduct in the Ca2+-free state compared to 3.3 in the Ca2+-liganded conformation.
source: On average only 1.8 lipids were present in the aqueduct in the Ca2+-free state compared to 3.3 the Ca2+-liganded conformation (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The observation that some lipids are located in the aqueduct even in the Ca2+-free conformation may be consistent with the observation that nhTMEM16 and afTMEM16 reconstituted into liposomes exhibit significant phospholipid scrambling in the absence of Ca2+.
source: The observation that some lipids are located in the aqueduct even in the Ca2+-free conformation may be consistent with the observation that nhTMEM16 and afTMEM16 reconstituted into liposomes exhibit significant phospholipid scrambling in the absence of Ca2+ (Malvezzi et al., 2013; Brunner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference connecting simulation observations to prior experimental findings cited in the literature.

claim: The greatest conformational change between Ca2+-liganded and Ca2+-free states is in the cytoplasmic half of TM6 (residues 451–470, RMSD = 10.6 Å) which moves away from TM7 and TM8.
source: The greatest change is in the cytoplasmic half of TM6 (residues 451–470, RMSD = 10.6 Å) which moves away from TM7 and TM8.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data comparing Ca2+-liganded and Ca2+-free states.

claim: Q468 in TM6 moves ~15 Å relative to TM7 and TM8 when Ca2+ is removed.
source: This movement is dramatic: Q468 moves ~15 Å relative to TM7 and TM8 which remain relatively constant.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data comparing Ca2+-liganded and Ca2+-free states.

claim: The conformational change observed in the extracellular half of TM4 (residues 325–345, RMSD = 5.1 Å) is likely responsible for gating.
source: More likely, the conformational change observed in the extracellular half of TM4 (residues 325–345, RMSD = 5.1 Å) which forms a narrow constriction of the aqueduct are responsible for gating.
evidence: This is an inference based on MD simulation data and structural analysis.

claim: F330 and T443 separate from 2.7 Å to 11.4 Å upon Ca2+ binding.
source: For example, F330 and T443 separate from 2.7 Å to 11.4 Å upon Ca2+ binding and T333 and Y439 separate from 2.6 Å to 6.1 Å (Figure 9C, Figure 9—video 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: T333 and Y439 separate from 2.6 Å to 6.1 Å upon Ca2+ binding.
source: For example, F330 and T443 separate from 2.7 Å to 11.4 Å upon Ca2+ binding and T333 and Y439 separate from 2.6 Å to 6.1 Å (Figure 9C, Figure 9—video 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Pinching of the aqueduct (distance <3 Å) at the level of T333 and Y439 occurs 40.3% of the time during the last 150 ns of the 1000 ns simulation in the absence of Ca2+.
source: Pinching of the aqueduct (distance <3 Å) at the level of T333 and Y439 occurs 40.3% of the time during the last 150 ns of the 1000 ns simulation in the absence of Ca2+ and only 6.3% of the time in the presence Ca2+ (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Pinching of the aqueduct at the level of T333 and Y439 occurs only 6.3% of the time in the presence of Ca2+.
source: Pinching of the aqueduct (distance <3 Å) at the level of T333 and Y439 occurs 40.3% of the time during the last 150 ns of the 1000 ns simulation in the absence of Ca2+ and only 6.3% of the time in the presence Ca2+ (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The aqueduct in the Ca2+-liganded conformation is fully hydrated throughout its entire length.
source: The aqueduct in the Ca2+-liganded conformation is fully hydrated throughout its entire length, as one would expect if these structures are providing an aqueous pathway for movement of hydrophilic lipid head groups.
evidence: This is based on analysis of MD simulation data.

claim: The aqueducts in the Ca2+-free conformation display markedly decreased hydration especially from the center of the membrane to the outer vestibule (0 < z < 10 Å).
source: In contrast, the aqueducts in the Ca2+-free conformation display markedly decreased hydration especially from the center of the membrane to the outer vestibule (0 < z < 10 Å) (Figure 10, Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of MD simulation data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The average number of water molecules in the aqueduct between z = 0–10 Å is decreased by >60% when Ca2+ is removed.
source: For example, the average number of water molecules in the aqueduct between z = 0–10 Å is decreased by >60% when Ca2+ is removed.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from MD simulation data.

claim: The structure of nhTMEM16 introduces a bend and a thinning of the lipid bilayer to reduce the energy barrier for hydrophilic head groups to move across the membrane.
source: First, the structure of the nhTMEM16 protein introduces a bend and a thinning of the lipid bilayer to reduce the energy barrier for hydrophilic head groups to move across the membrane.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the simulation data presented.

claim: The aqueduct provides a hydrophilic environment for head groups to translocate between leaflets while the hydrophobic acyl chains are stabilized by interactions with hydrophobic amino acids on the lips of the aqueduct as well as acyl chains of phospholipids in the hydrophobic phase of the bilayer.
source: Second, the aqueduct itself provides a hydrophilic environment for head groups to translocate between leaflets while the hydrophobic acyl chains are stabilized by interactions with hydrophobic amino acids on the lips of the aqueduct as well as acyl chains of phospholipids in the hydrophobic phase of the bilayer.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the simulation data presented.

claim: The constriction in the aqueduct plays a key role in gating scrambling by Ca2+.
source: We propose that this constriction plays a key role in gating scrambling by Ca2+ because this region (especially TM4) undergoes significant conformational changes in response to Ca2+ binding.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the simulation data and structural analysis.

claim: In the open conformation in the presence of Ca2+, water molecules in the gate region fill up the narrowest and deepest parts of the aqueduct and provide a water-filled pathway for spontaneous diffusion of lipid head groups.
source: In the open conformation in the presence of Ca2+, water molecules in the gate region fill up the narrowest and deepest parts of the aqueduct and provide a water-filled pathway for spontaneous diffusion of lipid head groups.
evidence: This is based on analysis of MD simulation data.

claim: The ion conductance of TMEM16F represents a leak of ions through the aqueduct that occurs during lipid scrambling.
source: The crystal structure of nhTMEM16 does not reveal an obvious alternative pathway for ion permeation through the bilayer other than the path taken by phospholipids (Hartzell and Whitlock, 2016) and we have proposed that the ion conductance of TMEM16F represents a leak of ions through the aqueduct that occurs during lipid scrambling (Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on structural analysis and prior work.

claim: Ion transport by scramblases is a leak current associated with lipid transport.
source: These data support the hypothesis that ion transport by scramblases is a leak current associated with lipid transport.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the simulation and experimental data presented.

claim: It seems unlikely that ion flux is necessary for phospholipid scrambling.
source: Because scrambling occurs in the absence of any ionic electrochemical driving force both in our simulations and our experiments, it seems unlikely that ion flux is necessary for phospholipid scrambling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation and experimental observations.

claim: Ion conduction by the Cl- channel TMEM16A likely occurs via a similar pathway to the one that conducts lipids in the TMEM16 scramblases.
source: It is likely that ion conduction by the Cl- channel TMEM16A occurs via a similar pathway to the one that conducts lipids in the TMEM16 scramblases (Hartzell and Whitlock, 2016; Jeng et al., 2016; Lim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior literature and the data presented.

claim: A low-resolution cryo-EM structure of the TMEM16A Cl- channel showed that the TMEM16A ion-conducting pore is enclosed by protein along ~2/3 of its length due to a structural rearrangement that brings TM4 and TM6 closer together.
source: Recently, a low-resolution cryo-EM structure of the TMEM16A Cl- channel was solved (Paulino et al., 2017) which showed that the TMEM16A ion-conducting pore, instead of being an open aqueduct as in nhTMEM16, is enclosed by protein along ~2/3 of its length due to a structural rearrangement that brings TM4 and TM6 closer together to enclose the pore.
evidence: This claim is based on a citation to a recently published cryo-EM structure.

claim: The structures of TMEM16A and nhTMEM16 are very similar aside from the pore enclosure.
source: Otherwise the structures of TMEM16A and nhTMEM16 are very similar.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the TMEM16A cryo-EM structure with the nhTMEM16 crystal structure.

claim: The V543S/T mutation might destabilize the interactions between TM4 and TM6 to open the pore to create an aqueduct in TMEM16A.
source: The V543S/T mutation might destabilize the interactions between TM4 and TM6 to open the pore to create an aqueduct.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of the mutation.

claim: The TMEM16A cryo-EM structure likely represents the inactivated state that TMEM16A enters in the presence of high Ca2+ concentrations.
source: It is unclear whether the TMEM16A cryo-EM structure is an open, ion-conducting conformation; the pore is not large enough to accommodate permeant ions except possibly Cl- (Fisher and Hartzell, 2017). It seems likely that the new structure represents the inactivated state that TMEM16A is known to enter in the presence of high Ca2+ concentrations used to purify the protein (Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis and prior knowledge about TMEM16A inactivation.

claim: nhTMEM16 tagged on the C-terminus with EGFP did not traffic to the plasma membrane.
source: Although nhTMEM16 tagged on the C-terminus with EGFP did not traffic to the plasma membrane (Brunner et al., 2014), nhTMEM16 tagged on the N-terminus with 3X-FLAG or untagged nhTMEM16 did traffic to the plasma membrane (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation and a citation to prior work.

claim: nhTMEM16 tagged on the N-terminus with 3X-FLAG or untagged nhTMEM16 did traffic to the plasma membrane.
source: Although nhTMEM16 tagged on the C-terminus with EGFP did not traffic to the plasma membrane (Brunner et al., 2014), nhTMEM16 tagged on the N-terminus with 3X-FLAG or untagged nhTMEM16 did traffic to the plasma membrane (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Most cells expressing WT nhTMEM16 had scrambled by 15 min after elevating cytosolic Ca2+ by establishing whole cell recording.
source: Most cells expressing WT nhTMEM16 had scrambled by 15 min after elevating cytosolic Ca2+ by establishing whole cell recording.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation.

claim: No scrambling was observed with WT nhTMEM16 expressing cells patch clamped with zero Ca2+ during the same time period.
source: No scrambling was observed with WT nhTMEM16 expressing cells patch clamped with zero Ca2+ during the same time period.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation.

claim: This result differs from that reported for purified fungal TMEM16 proteins reconstituted in liposomes that show substantial scramblase activity in the absence of Ca2+.
source: This result differs from that reported for purified fungal TMEM16 proteins reconstituted in liposomes that show substantial scramblase activity in the absence of Ca2+ (Malvezzi et al., 2013; Brunner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior experimental findings cited in the literature.

claim: Less than 20% of untransfected cells scramble under similar conditions.
source: Less than 20% of untransfected cells scramble under similar conditions, as we reported previously (Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on prior experimental observation cited.

claim: Untransfected HEK cells express low levels of TMEM16F that may be responsible for scrambling in a small fraction of cells.
source: While this has not been explored systematically, untransfected HEK cells express low levels of TMEM16F that may be responsible for scrambling in a small fraction of cells.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential explanation for background scrambling.

claim: The slow time course of scrambling by nhTMEM16 is similar to that previously described for TMEM16F.
source: This slow time course of scrambling is similar to that previously described for TMEM16F (Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior experimental findings cited in the literature.

claim: The slow time course of scrambling is explained partly by the sensitivity of the Annexin-V binding assay, but apparently also involves a regulatory step we do not understand.
source: It is explained partly by the sensitivity of the Annexin-V binding assay, but apparently also involves a regulatory step we do not understand.
evidence: This is an inference and acknowledgment of incomplete understanding.

claim: The X-ray crystallographic structure of fungal nhTMEM16 (4WIT) at 3.4 Å resolution was used as the starting structure for simulation.
source: The X-ray crystallographic structure of fungal nhTMEM16 (4WIT) at 3.4 Å resolution (Brunner et al., 2016) was used as the starting structure for simulation.
evidence: This describes the starting structure for the MD simulations.

claim: Missing loops in the nhTMEM16 structure were added using SuperLooper.
source: Missing loops (residues 1–18, 130–140, 465–482, 586–593, 657–659, 685–691 and 720–735) were added using SuperLooper (Hildebrand et al., 2009) which models loops based on templates from protein structures to fill in gaps in the protein structure.
evidence: This describes a computational method used to prepare the structure for simulation.

claim: The protein was embedded into an asymmetric lipid bilayer with the outer leaflet composed of pure POPC and the inner leaflet a 2:1 POPC/POPS mixture.
source: The protein was embedded into an asymmetric lipid bilayer that was generated using the CHARMM-GUI membrane builder (Wu et al., 2014). The outer leaflet was composed of pure POPC (palmitoyl-oleoyl phosphatidylcholine), while the inner leaflet was a 2:1 POPC/POPS (palmitoyl-oleoyl phosphatidylserine) mixture to mimic eukaryotic plasma membranes.
evidence: This describes the simulation system setup.

claim: MD simulations were carried out with NAMD2.9 using CHARMM-CMAP and CHARMM36 parameters.
source: MD simulations were carried out with NAMD2.9 (Phillips et al., 2005) using CHARMM-CMAP (Mackerell et al., 2004) and CHARMM36 (Klauda et al., 2010) parameters set to model the proteins and lipids, respectively.
evidence: This describes the computational methods used for the simulations.

claim: HEK-293 cells were purchased from ATCC in 2002 and were authenticated using STR profiling.
source: HEK-293 cells were purchased (frozen) from ATCC in 2002 (catalogue number CRL-1573) and were authenticated using STR profiling.
evidence: This describes the cell line used in experiments.

claim: Tests for mycoplasma in HEK-293 cells were negative.
source: Tests for mycoplasma were negative.
evidence: This describes quality control of the cell line used in experiments.
